reference.source: GeneReviews POLG-Related Disorders / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: The classic clinical triad is intractable epilepsy (often with epilepsia partialis continua), psychomotor regression and liver disease progressing to failure
It is an autosomal recessive nuclear disorder caused by biallelic mutations in POLG, the gene for the catalytic subunit of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, leading to mitochondrial DNA depletion
Sodium valproate must be avoided because it can precipitate or accelerate fulminant hepatic failure in POLG disease, and this warning applies whenever POLG is suspected before genetic confirmation
Seizures are frequently occipital in onset, drug-resistant, and can evolve into status epilepticus
Liver involvement may be present at onset or emerge later, sometimes only after valproate exposure, and includes microvesicular steatosis and eventual cirrhosis
Cerebrospinal fluid protein is often raised, and MRI may show occipital and thalamic changes; EEG can show high-amplitude, low-frequency activity with polyspikes
Management is supportive, targeting seizure control with mitochondria-sparing agents, nutritional and hepatic support, avoiding hepatotoxic and mitochondrial-toxic drugs
reference.pathophysiology: Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is caused by recessive mutations in POLG, which encodes the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase gamma, the sole polymerase responsible for replicating and repairing mitochondrial DNA. Defective enzyme activity leads to quantitative depletion and qualitative errors of mitochondrial DNA, particularly in post-mitotic tissues with high energy demand such as neurons and hepatocytes. The resulting failure of oxidative phosphorylation causes progressive neuronal loss, spongiform change in grey matter and hepatocellular injury. Valproate further inhibits mitochondrial function and fatty acid oxidation, which explains its propensity to trigger catastrophic liver failure in these patients.
additionalDifferentials: Non-metabolic causes of intractable childhood epilepsy with regression
Wilson disease and other metabolic liver diseases
Acute viral or autoimmune hepatitis with encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: POLG molecular testing as the definitive diagnostic step
Liver function tests with coagulation profile to detect synthetic hepatic failure
EEG to characterise occipital and multifocal epileptiform activity
Brain MRI looking for occipital, thalamic and cerebellar signal change and volume loss
Blood lactate and, where indicated, quantification of mitochondrial DNA content or muscle respiratory-chain enzymology
redFlags: Refractory seizures or status epilepticus, including epilepsia partialis continua
Rising transaminases, coagulopathy or jaundice indicating hepatic failure
Recent valproate exposure with clinical deterioration
reference.prognosis: Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is relentlessly progressive with a poor prognosis; most affected children deteriorate over months to a few years, and liver failure, often accelerated by valproate, is a major cause of death.
pitfalls: Giving sodium valproate for the epilepsy before excluding POLG disease, risking fatal hepatotoxicity
Attributing the liver failure to the anticonvulsant alone and missing the underlying mitochondrial disorder
Waiting for liver disease before considering the diagnosis, since hepatic involvement can be delayed
Considering liver transplantation without recognising the systemic, progressive neurological disease
management: Avoid sodium valproate whenever POLG disease is suspected, even before genetic confirmation, as it can trigger fulminant hepatic failure
Treat the drug-resistant, often occipital-onset seizures with alternative antiseizure medications and manage status epilepticus under neurology guidance
Provide supportive nutritional, respiratory and physiotherapy care for progressive psychomotor regression
Monitor liver function tests and coagulation to detect emerging or valproate-triggered hepatic synthetic failure
Avoid liver transplantation in most cases given the underlying multisystem mitochondrial disease and poor neurological prognosis
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic, neurology and palliative care as the disorder progresses
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
